name: Programming Languages
description: The languages programmers write in, from assembly, Fortran and C to Python, JavaScript and Rust, in the order they appeared.

checkpoints.name: Machine code and assembly
checkpoints.note: The first programmers give machines their instructions as numbers. Assembly language, from 1949, lets them write short names instead, one line for each step the machine takes.

checkpoints.name: The first high-level languages
checkpoints.note: Fortran, Lisp, ALGOL and COBOL show that a computer can understand human-style instructions. BASIC opens programming to students, and each of these languages has descendants still in use.

checkpoints.name: C and structured programming
checkpoints.note: Pascal, C, Smalltalk, SQL and Prolog set out new ways to organise programs and data. C becomes the language of Unix, and with it much of the world's software.

checkpoints.name: Object-oriented languages
checkpoints.note: C++ and Objective-C bring object-oriented programming to ordinary work, Perl becomes a tool for gluing systems together, Microsoft's Visual Basic makes Windows programs easy to build, and Python and Haskell start quietly.

checkpoints.name: The web era
checkpoints.note: Java, JavaScript, PHP and Ruby all arrive in 1995 as the web creates demand for new languages. Microsoft answers Java with C#, and Scratch, from MIT, teaches children to program with blocks.

checkpoints.name: Modern languages
checkpoints.note: Go, Rust, Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript aim at safety and speed. Each fixes a pain point of an older language, and none has replaced the old ones, which still run much of the world's software.
